supportingExcerpt: Lineage describes descent from earlier cells. A cell type or identity describes a differentiated family, while a state describes context-dependent features such as activation, stress or cycling. A genetic clone has shared ancestry and can be tracked through specified genomic features; an RNA cluster alone does not establish that ancestry. Stem cells can renew and generate descendants; progenitor potential is restricted by the biological context. Differentiation develops specialized properties without requiring every change of state to become a new lineage.

In a fictional set with separately established shared genetic ancestry, one cell is cycling and another is noncycling. Different activity labels do not require different ancestry. Conversely, two cells in the same RNA cluster need not belong to the same genetic clone. The origin of the ancestry label matters: expression resemblance alone does not establish it.

Support a malignant-cell assignment with tissue context, a coherent marker panel, suitable normal references and quality checks, rather than one marker or cluster name. In five primary glioblastomas, Patel and colleagues profiled 430 cells and inferred broad chromosome alterations by averaging RNA expression along chromosomes against normal reference profiles. This was RNA-based inference, not a direct DNA copy count or a breast diagnostic rule. A flat inferred profile can miss a malignant cell lacking a detectable broad change; focal alterations and point mutations can also be missed. Matched DNA, pathology and spatial evidence can corroborate an assignment, but bulk DNA does not identify every RNA barcode. Mixed markers may reflect ambient RNA or doublets. In another fictional mixed sample, vimentin RNA could come from fibroblasts or a changed cancer-cell programme. Even cell-attributed expression of that marker alone does not establish invasion, resistance or ancestry. Keep uncertain assignments uncertain.

The nucleus houses most cellular DNA; mitochondria have their own genome and participate in energy metabolism and other processes. Ribosomes make polypeptide chains. The endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi process and sort selected membrane or secreted cargo, while lysosomes degrade delivered material in an acidic compartment. That itinerary is not the route of every protein. Cytosol is the fluid outside membrane-bound organelle interiors; cytoplasm includes cytosol and structures outside the nucleus. A vesicle lumen is not cytosol.

A lipid bilayer and its proteins separate the cell from its surroundings. Permeability depends on size, charge and chemical properties, rather than a universal small-molecule versus antibody rule. Passive movement follows the relevant gradient; active transport uses energy directly or through a coupled gradient. Endocytosis encloses material in a membrane-bound compartment. Delivery to cytosol or another target compartment requires further steps. Cytosol is fluid outside organelle interiors; cytoplasm includes that fluid and structures outside the nucleus.

Among cytosolic ribosomes, some are free and others sit on the cytosolic face of rough ER, outside its lumen. Consider one secreted protein: it enters the ER lumen during synthesis, travels through the lumens of transport vesicles and Golgi compartments, and can leave when a secretory vesicle fuses with the cell membrane. Movement within these membrane-enclosed spaces is not cytosolic escape. This selected route does not describe every protein; a compartment diagram alone does not measure transport, activity or treatment effect.
Localization, colocalization, amount, interaction and function need different evidence. More or brighter organelle staining does not by itself measure the rate of material passing through a pathway.

In an inward-budding uptake example, an open pocket remains continuous with extracellular fluid until it pinches off. Once sealed, the vesicle is inside the cell but its contents are still in a membrane-enclosed lumen rather than free in cytosol. A process arrow does not make the cargo cross the bilayer. A receptor can span the membrane and bind a ligand outside; binding alone does not establish internalisation, cytosolic delivery or signalling.

Surface-associated fluorescence does not establish internalization or cytosolic delivery. A membrane-exclusion dye tests the integrity property resolved by that assay; it does not certify every cell function.

In an invented sequence example, AACGT can carry a methyl group on its C while the underlying base order remains AACGT. Replacing that C with T instead gives AATGT, a different underlying DNA sequence. Changing a chemical mark on a histone protein is different again. Keep that biological comparison separate from an assay that chemically converts bases: standard bisulfite treatment can change the readout without establishing that the original DNA carried a C-to-T variant. Read the conversion chemistry, locus and cell context before interpreting a methylation call.

DNA methylation changes a base’s chemical state without substituting the underlying sequence letter. Much human methylation analysis concerns 5-methylcytosine at CpG sites. Histone modifications affect DNA-associated proteins and are distinct from marks on DNA itself. Some regulatory states persist through division; epigenetic does not mean every mark is permanent or transmitted between generations. Promoter methylation can participate in reduced transcription, while patterns elsewhere need their own interpretation.

Standard bisulfite analysis changes unmodified cytosine but reads both 5-methylcytosine and 5-hydroxymethylcytosine as C. Oxidative bisulfite methods separate those features through additional chemistry. Ordinary amplified DNA sequence does not preserve this direct chemical measurement.

A methylation signal in mixed tissue is not a percentage of cancer cells with a silenced gene. Cell mixture, genomic location, conversion controls and method resolution matter. Association with low RNA does not establish causation or treatment sensitivity.

Inherited germline variants came through an egg or sperm and are generally present across many tissues. A de novo constitutional variant need not have been inherited from a parent. Changes arising after fertilization can create mosaic distributions. Somatic variants occur in body-cell lineages, including normal tissues as well as cancers. Origin, distribution, harmfulness and transmissibility are separate questions; neither a variant class nor a large read fraction settles them.

In two invented histories, an early constitutional variant may be inherited or de novo, whereas a later variant can mark a mosaic body-cell lineage, including a normal blood clone. A partial set of sampled cells leaves reproductive-cell involvement and unsampled tumour-cell genotypes unknown. Suppose a cartoon contains two marked blood cells among four and four marked DNA fragments among eight. Those are counts of chosen symbols, not measured allele fractions, a tumour fraction or evidence of inheritance. Plasma fragments are not intact circulating cells, and arrows from blood cells or tumour cells describe possible DNA contributions, not an exhaustive source map or proof of a particular fragment's origin.

Cell-free DNA (cfDNA) is DNA outside intact cells in a specimen. Circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) is the tumour-derived part of the plasma DNA mixture, rather than a different material competing with cfDNA. DNA from non-tumour tissues can contribute much of that mixture, as illustrated by Moss and colleagues' methylation-atlas study. Total extracted DNA is therefore not a tumour measurement. A finite evaluated aliquot can contain no qualifying tumour signal even when disease exists elsewhere.

Liquid biopsy describes a specimen approach. A test may track known tumour features, look for predefined mutation, methylation or fragment patterns, or profile detectable alterations. Its target coverage, origin checks, sample requirements and calling rule determine the claim. Genotyping, residual-disease monitoring and screening have different intended uses; a method label does not validate every use or locate the source of a plasma signal.

Yield is not origin: in a fictional experiment equal 1 mL plasma aliquots give 2 and 4 nanograms of cfDNA and no tumour-attributed signal is reported. Total DNA doubled, but tumour fraction and any tumour-DNA fold change cannot be calculated because tumour attribution was not measured. A fragment's source needs evidence such as paired white-blood-cell and tumour sequencing (Razavi 2019), and a variant seen in plasma is not automatically tumour-derived.
VAF is the proportion of usable reads or assay-defined molecules supporting the alternate sequence; keep the denominator: 25 of 100 usable observations is 25%.

Read-based VAF divides variant-supporting reads by informative reads at the locus. Some assays instead report a molecule-based measure, so keep the laboratory’s definition. Tumor purity, local allele-specific copy number, ploidy, subclonal mixture and assay behavior affect the value. VAF alone cannot assign zygosity, variant origin, the number of clones or a cancer-cell percentage. Changes over time in plasma also require attention to specimen and non-tumor DNA contributors.

A protein-coding gene supplies RNA that can be translated into a polypeptide, while a noncoding RNA gene produces a functional RNA. Promoters and other regulatory regions influence transcription in a cell-dependent context. One gene can have several transcript versions. Exons are retained regions of a specified processed transcript and can include untranslated sequence; introns are removed by splicing. Coding sequence is the translated part of a coding message. A gene name alone does not specify a transcript, coding interval or protein product.

RNA, short for ribonucleic acid, uses ribose and usually uracil in place of DNA’s thymine. It is often single-stranded but can fold through internal pairing. Messenger RNA carries a coding template; ribosomal RNA contributes to ribosome structure and catalysis; transfer RNA brings amino acids; regulatory RNAs influence other molecules. Many nuclear messages receive a 5-prime cap and poly(A) tail and have introns removed by splicing before translation, but these features are not universal to all RNAs. Ribosomes read a coding sequence in codons to produce a polypeptide; processing, folding and localization follow.

Nonsense-mediated decay is RNA surveillance coupled to translation termination. Splicing can leave exon junction protein complexes near later joins in the message. Translation can remove junction-associated proteins; early termination while an appropriate complex remains downstream can help recruit decay machinery in one human route. Stop position, exon architecture, proximity to the start and other transcript features affect susceptibility. A common junction-distance shortcut is a hypothesis, not a universal clinical cutoff.

Human-cancer analyses found that a model containing several rules described RNA effects better than the junction rule alone; compensation could mask loss at gene level. Test the relevant transcript or allele with controls for RNA quality and cell mixture. Protein identity, persistence and function need separate measurements: RNA decay is distinct from protein degradation.

Variable, diversity and joining segments provide the V, D and J names. Antibody heavy and conventional T-cell-receptor beta chains use VDJ arrangements; antibody light and T-cell-receptor alpha chains use VJ. RAG1/RAG2 recognize recombination signals and initiate DNA cutting; classical non-homologous end-joining repair machinery processes and joins coding ends, adding sequence diversity. Purified-protein cutting experiments and RAG1-deficient mouse experiments established distinct mechanistic requirements. RAG proteins are not the general repair machinery for every DNA break.

Rearrangement occurs in developing lymphocyte lineages, rather than changing receptor genes in every body cell. Some joins are unproductive; expression and developmental selection are further steps. Later antibody mutation and class switching are different processes.

Receptor-gene joining, expression, developmental selection and response by mature lymphocytes are separate questions. In T-cell development, selection involves recognition of self peptides bound to MHC in the thymus; describing gene assembly as preceding a later antigen-driven response must not imply that development is free of antigen interactions. Choosing V2, D1 and J3 in an invented example states a selected rearrangement, not an observed segment count or a receptor deliberately built for an encountered antigen. A RAG variant in mixed tissue does not establish active receptor rearrangement in epithelial cells.
Receptor sequence or clonality does not establish antigen specificity, tumor recognition or malignant diagnosis. RAG RNA/protein presence alone does not establish active recombination.

Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

In an invented comparison, two related protein forms R1 and R2 both contain the same short amino-acid sequence, but R2 lacks a region present in R1. Detecting that shared peptide after digestion does not distinguish the intact forms or prove their activity. Folding changes the chain's arrangement in space without changing its residue order; cutting off a terminal segment is a different processing example and is not required for every protein. Neither a sequence that could yield a peptide nor its measurement in a digest establishes display by HLA.

An antibody may recognize an epitope on more than one product form or a remaining fragment. Many mass-spectrometry workflows digest proteins into peptides: a shared detected peptide cannot distinguish every full-length form. A candidate peptide sequence also does not establish its display by HLA. Separate assays address amount, location, intact form, function and antigen presentation.

Primary structure describes sequence; secondary structure describes local arrangements; tertiary structure describes a chain’s organization; quaternary structure describes assembly between chains. These are levels of description, rather than four obligatory stages. A domain is a recognizable structural unit; a motif is a recurring sequence or structural pattern. An interface is a contact surface and can combine residues far apart in sequence. Intrinsically disordered regions can have normal functions without one stable isolated fold.

Experimental structures reflect particular preparations and conditions, and may omit flexible regions. In AlphaFold2, pLDDT concerns local structural confidence, while predicted aligned error helps assess uncertainty in relative region placement. A confident domain cannot certify a proposed inter-domain pocket or contact. Neither score measures binding affinity, protein abundance, a variant’s functional effect or clinical benefit.

X-ray crystallography interprets diffraction from crystals; crystallization and flexible regions constrain what can be resolved. NMR uses signals and spatial restraints, often in solution, and can report an ensemble of compatible structures. Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy combines many projections of particles preserved in ice into a three-dimensional map. Each route requires preparation, experimental data and model interpretation. Check the method, local support, missing regions and validation of the actual structure; an atomic-looking model is not a direct photograph of every molecular state or proof of binding or function.

For a short invented duplex, 5-prime ATCG 3-prime pairs with 3-prime TAGC 5-prime. The paired bases sit between sugar-phosphate backbones, and nuclear DNA can wrap around histone cores to form nucleosomes. A gene occupies a region of DNA, not the entire chromosome. A packaging cartoon does not establish one universal 30 nm fibre, an X-shaped chromosome at every stage, copy number or gene activity.

DNA contains nucleotide chains with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases A, T, C and G. Complementary A–T and C–G pairing joins antiparallel strands. Nuclear chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins as chromatin; nucleosomes organize DNA around histones. Mitochondria carry a separate genome. A gene is a functional region within DNA, rather than an entire chromosome. Replication copies DNA, while transcription produces RNA from a selected template. Packaging and gene presence do not establish active transcription or a functional protein.
